960.hook: the Chmielnicki uprising destroys Jewish communities in Ukraine
960.howItsDone: Jews remember the massacres of 1648 in chronicles, memorial prayers and laments, and some communities long kept a fast day for them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, England: a door left unlocked, and Jews quietly readmitted. Your line was readmitted. A new week begins, and it begins far to the east, with a hard memory. Go gently today. Day nine hundred sixty.

Jewish memory has its own way of naming years. In the Hebrew calendar, years are written with letters, and two short letter-words, tach and tat, came to stand for a time of terror in Poland and Ukraine. Jews spoke of the decrees of tach and tat the way other people say a date they cannot forget. In the ordinary calendar, the first of those years is a single number. It is today's word.
screen: `YEARS WRITTEN IN LETTERS.` → `TACH AND TAT.` → `A NUMBER THAT IS A MEMORY.`

segments.voice: In the lands of Ukraine then ruled by Poland, the Cossacks rose up under a leader named Bohdan Chmielnicki. The uprising had its own grievances, against Polish lords and their power over the land and the people who worked it. Jews were caught in the middle. Some served the lords as stewards and leaseholders, collecting rents and running mills and inns, and so in the rebels' eyes they stood for the lords. As the rebel forces moved through towns, Jewish communities were attacked and destroyed. People fled to fortified towns, and some of those towns fell. Families were killed, taken captive, or forced to convert. The chronicles of the time give large numbers, and historians still argue over them. What no one disputes is that whole communities disappeared. A survivor named Nathan Hannover wrote a chronicle of those years. He gave it a title from the Psalms, from a cry of someone drowning: "I am sunk in deep mire, where there is no standing." In Hebrew, deep mire is yeven metzulah, and that became the book's name. He wrote it in plain Hebrew, so that people would know what had happened, town by town. Afterward, the rabbis of Poland set aside a day of fasting and lament, and some communities kept it long afterward. A massacre in these lessons is not a plot twist. It is a number that stands for real people, names mostly lost, held in a people's memory. That is what 1648 means here.
screen: `AN UPRISING AGAINST POLISH LORDS.` · `JEWS CAUGHT IN THE MIDDLE.` · `WHOLE COMMUNITIES DESTROYED.` · `DEEP MIRE, WHERE THERE IS NO STANDING.` · then, large: `1648.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: remember a massacre in silence. Sit still. Let your breathing slow, and let your hands rest open. You don't need to picture anything violent. Just hold in mind that there were towns, and in them families: someone baking bread, a child learning letters, an old man at prayer. Let the silence be for them. If thoughts come, let them pass. If you pray, you can remember them in your own words, or with no words at all. The bell holds the time.
1648. The year the Chmielnicki uprising began, when Jewish communities in Ukraine were destroyed; remembered in Hebrew as the decrees of tach and tat. Today's word.

961.title: Shabbetai Tzvi
961.hook: a would-be messiah stirs the Jewish world, then converts to Islam
961.howItsDone: Traditional Jewish daily prayer still asks for the coming of the messiah, and Jewish tradition remembers Shabbetai Tzvi as a warning to hope carefully and to test such claims.

segments.voice: Yesterday, 1648: deep mire, and whole communities lost. Did you pause for a date tied to loss? Today, a hope that rose out of a hard time and swept across the Jewish world. Day nine hundred sixty-one.

A merchant packs barrels and sends them to his son's house in Hamburg. Linen, dried peas, beans, dried meat, all sealed and ready, because any day now word may come to leave for the Land of Israel. His daughter-in-law, Glückel of Hameln, the memoir writer we met not long ago, wrote about those barrels. They sat in her house, packed and waiting, for a long time, while the family went on with ordinary life around them. The news he was waiting for was about one man. Today, his name.
screen: `BARRELS PACKED IN HAMBURG.` → `READY TO LEAVE AT ANY MOMENT.` → `WAITING FOR ONE MAN.`

segments.voice: Shabbetai Tzvi was a scholar from Smyrna, in the Ottoman lands, a man of strange moods and striking presence. A young teacher named Nathan of Gaza declared that Shabbetai was the messiah, and Shabbetai, who had hinted at such a claim years before, embraced it. The news traveled by letter, port to port, from the Land of Israel to Amsterdam, Hamburg and Poland. Some communities added prayers for him. Some people sold homes and businesses. Others fasted and repented, or danced in the streets. After years of grief, the hope felt close enough to touch. The Hebrew word at the center is mashiach. It means anointed. In the Tanakh, kings and priests were anointed with oil, and over time the word came to name a king from David's line who would bring the exiles home. Then the Ottoman authorities arrested him. He was brought before the sultan's court and given a choice, and he converted to Islam. For his followers the news was a shock. Some left him in grief and shame. Some insisted the conversion was a hidden part of his mission, and kept believing. Rabbis who had warned against him from the start were proven right in their own eyes. Jewish tradition now calls him a false messiah: not a liar about the hope, but a man whose claim did not come true. The hope itself remained. The prophet Habakkuk had said of the promised vision, "though it tarry, wait for it." The lesson some drew was not to stop waiting, but to wait more carefully.
screen: `NATHAN OF GAZA'S DECLARATION.` · `LETTERS FROM PORT TO PORT.` · `MASHIACH: ANOINTED.` · `BEFORE THE SULTAN'S COURT.` · then, large: `FALSE MESSIAH.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: hope carefully. Sit, and breathe slowly. Think of one thing you are hoping for right now, something you want badly. Hold it for a moment without pushing it away. Then ask two quiet questions. What would it mean to keep this hope, even if it takes longer than I want? And what would I lose if I gave up everything else for it today? Let both answers sit side by side. If you pray, you can bring your hope with you in your own words. The bell holds the time.
Shabbetai Tzvi. A scholar from Smyrna proclaimed as messiah, who stirred Jewish communities everywhere his letters reached, and then converted to Islam. Today's word.
Your line: false messiah. Today, when a promise sounds too good, wait one more day before you pack your barrels. Day nine hundred sixty-one.

962.title: After the fall
962.hook: despair, and slowly new movements of piety and learning
962.howItsDone: Luzzatto's The Path of the Upright is still studied in yeshivas and study groups, often slowly, a chapter at a time, as a guide to character.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shabbetai Tzvi, the man proclaimed messiah who converted to Islam. Your line was false messiah. Did you wait a day before believing something too good? Today, what came after. Day nine hundred sixty-two.

Back in Hamburg, the barrels are still standing in Glückel's house. Linen, peas, dried meat, packed for a journey that is not going to happen. In her telling, they waited a long while, and in the end they were opened and the food used up. It's a small, almost ordinary scene. Someone has to decide when to unpack. Someone has to cook the beans meant for the road. That moment, multiplied across a whole people, is today's word.
screen: `THE BARRELS, STILL PACKED.` → `A JOURNEY THAT WON'T HAPPEN.` → `SOMEONE HAS TO UNPACK.`

segments.voice: When the news of Shabbetai Tzvi's conversion spread, the first thing that came was shame and grief. People had sold homes, fasted, announced the end of exile, and now had to face their neighbors. Some of his followers kept believing in secret, which kept rabbis wary long afterward. Teachers grew suspicious of anyone claiming special revelation, and some communities limited the study of mystical texts to older, learned students. The rabbis also had an old warning to lean on. The Talmud, in tractate Sanhedrin, speaks harshly of those who calculate the end, because when the date passes, people lose hope altogether. The point was not to stop hoping. It was to stop setting dates. And then, slowly, something grew in the space the disappointment left. Not a new announcement, but a turn inward and toward steady work. An Italian kabbalist, Moshe Chaim Luzzatto, wrote a book called The Path of the Upright. It takes an old rabbinic teaching, a ladder of qualities that starts with watchfulness and zeal and climbs toward holiness, and walks up it one rung at a time, with plain advice for ordinary days. In Eastern Europe, new circles of prayer and learning were forming, and one of them would soon change Jewish life. The Psalms had already spoken to this kind of night: "Weeping may tarry for the night, but joy cometh in the morning." After the fall, there was no single morning. There was a slow dawn, built by people who unpacked their barrels and kept going.
screen: `SHAME AND GRIEF.` · `STOP SETTING DATES.` · `A LADDER, ONE RUNG AT A TIME.` · `NEW CIRCLES IN THE EAST.` · then, large: `JOY COMETH IN THE MORNING.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: recover from one disappointment. Sit, and let your breath find its own pace. Bring to mind one thing that didn't happen the way you hoped. Not the biggest one; something you can hold. Notice what you packed for it: plans, money, words you'd already said. Then ask: what is one barrel I could unpack today? One plan to let go of, one thing to put to ordinary use. You don't have to feel fine about it. Just take one rung. If you pray, you can bring the disappointment with you in your own words. The bell holds the time.
After the fall. The time after Shabbetai Tzvi's conversion: grief and caution first, then slowly new movements of piety and learning. Today's word.
Your line: after disappointment. Today, take one small step on something that let you down: one rung, not the whole ladder. Day nine hundred sixty-two.

963.title: The Council of Four Lands
963.hook: Polish Jewry governed itself through an elected council
963.howItsDone: Jewish communities today still run their own synagogues, schools, burial societies and charities through boards and committees chosen by their members.

segments.voice: Yesterday, after the fall: barrels unpacked, and a slow dawn. Your line was after disappointment. Did you take one rung? Today we turn to Eastern Europe, and to how its Jews ran their own affairs. Day nine hundred sixty-three.

The fair at Lublin is loud. Wagons of grain and cloth, horses being traded, merchants shouting prices in several languages. Jewish traders are everywhere, doing business. But in a room off the market, a different kind of meeting is under way. Rabbis and community leaders from across the region sit around a table with ledgers and letters. They are not here to sell anything. They are here to govern. Today's word is the name of that table.
screen: `THE FAIR AT LUBLIN.` → `A ROOM OFF THE MARKET.` → `LEADERS AROUND A TABLE.`

segments.voice: In the kingdom of Poland and Lithuania, Jews lived in their own communities, each called a kehillah, with its own leaders, courts and charities. Above them, Polish Jewry built something larger: a council of regional leaders, chosen by their communities, who met regularly at the great fairs, where people traveled anyway. It was called in Hebrew the Va'ad Arba Aratzot, the Council of Four Lands, after the regions it spoke for. What did it do? The crown demanded taxes from the Jews as a group, and the council divided that bill among the communities. It settled quarrels between towns. It made rules for trade, for schools, for the printing of books, and for ransoming captives, which mattered terribly after the hard years we heard about earlier this week. And it spoke for Polish Jews before the king and his officials. The idea underneath is older. In the Torah, Moses tries to judge every case himself, from morning to evening, until his father-in-law Jethro tells him he will wear himself out, and advises him to choose capable, trustworthy people to share the work. Hillel, in the Mishnah, adds a short warning: don't separate yourself from the community. Self-governing does not mean free of the king. The council worked inside a kingdom that could change the rules. But for a long time, Polish Jews collected their own taxes, judged their own disputes and taught their own children, through people they had chosen. In the end the Polish government dissolved the council, and the kehillot carried on without it.
screen: `EACH TOWN A KEHILLAH.` · `MEETING AT THE GREAT FAIRS.` · `TAXES, QUARRELS, BOOKS, CAPTIVES.` · `JETHRO: SHARE THE WORK.` · then, large: `SELF-GOVERNING.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: take part in your community. Sit, and breathe. Picture the groups you belong to: a street, a congregation, a school, a team, a family chat. Ask which one could use a little more of you. Not everything; one hour, one job, one meeting where your voice would help. Moses learned he couldn't carry it all; someone else may be carrying too much right now. Let one concrete idea come to you. If you pray, you can pray for that community in your own words. The bell holds the time.
The Council of Four Lands. The council of chosen leaders through which Polish Jewry governed its own affairs: taxes, disputes, books and captives. Today's word.
screen: `THE COUNCIL OF FOUR LANDS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: self-governing. Today, show up for one small piece of a shared life: a meeting, a sign-up sheet, a neighbor's question. Day nine hundred sixty-three.

964.title: The Baal Shem Tov's life
964.hook: a healer and teacher who walked the Carpathian forests
964.howItsDone: Hasidim retell the tales of the Baal Shem Tov's life at meals, gatherings and on the anniversary of his passing, and some make pilgrimages to his grave in Medzhybizh.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Council of Four Lands, leaders around a table at the fair. Your line was self-governing. Did you show up for one piece of a shared life? Today, a man who spent his young years far from any council table. Day nine hundred sixty-four.

High in the Carpathian mountains, a man is digging clay out of a hillside. Every so often his wife comes with a cart, loads what he has dug, and takes it down to town to sell. Then he goes back into the trees, alone, for days at a time. He prays there. He studies there. Nobody in the valley thinks of him as anyone special. The stories about him say that was exactly how he wanted it. Today, his life.
screen: `DIGGING CLAY IN THE MOUNTAINS.` → `HIS WIFE TAKES IT TO TOWN.` → `ALONE IN THE TREES.`

segments.voice: Israel ben Eliezer became known as the Baal Shem Tov. Earlier on this path we heard his teaching. Today we hear the life the stories tell, mostly from a book of tales collected by people who loved him, In Praise of the Baal Shem Tov. Historians handle it carefully; it is memory and legend woven together. In the tales, he is orphaned as a small child. His dying father tells him to fear nothing but God. As a boy, he keeps slipping away from school into the forest. As a young man, he works as a teacher's helper, walking the little children to school and back, singing with them along the way. Later he is a caretaker in a house of study, and people take him for a simple man, while at night he learns alone. Then come the hidden years. He and his wife live in the mountains, he digs clay and lime, she sells it, and he spends long days in the forests in prayer and solitude. Only later, the tales say, does he reveal himself as a teacher. A baal shem, a master of the Name, was a familiar figure in Jewish villages then: a healer who wrote amulets and gave remedies of herbs. He was known first as one of these, a healer the poor could reach. Then students came for the teaching, and he settled in the town of Medzhybizh. The Psalms say, "The heavens declare the glory of God." The tales suggest that before he taught anyone, the forest taught him: the trees, the streams, the long silence.
screen: `ORPHANED, TOLD TO FEAR ONLY GOD.` · `A TEACHER'S HELPER, SINGING.` · `HIDDEN YEARS IN THE MOUNTAINS.` · `A HEALER THE POOR COULD REACH.` · then, large: `IN THE FORESTS.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: find a teacher in nature. If you can, sit near a window or step outside. If not, close your eyes and bring to mind a tree, a sky, or water you know well. Breathe slowly and simply watch. What does it do? A tree stays put and grows. Water finds its way around things. The sky holds weather without becoming it. Let one of them teach you one thing for today. If you pray, you can give thanks in your own words for what you see. The bell holds the time.
The Baal Shem Tov's life. An orphan, a teacher's helper, a clay digger in the mountains, a healer, and then a teacher, as the tales remember him. Today's word.
screen: `THE BAAL SHEM TOV'S LIFE — today's word`.

965.title: Hasidism spreads
965.hook: the Maggid's students carry the movement across Eastern Europe
965.howItsDone: Hasidim travel to their rebbe for Shabbat and holidays, gather at the rebbe's tish to hear teaching and sing niggunim, and study the books of the Maggid's students, such as the Tanya.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Baal Shem Tov's life: the orphan, the clay digger, the healer. Your line was in the forests. Did a tree or a sky teach you anything? Today, what happened to his teaching after him. Day nine hundred sixty-five.

A muddy road in Galicia, the day before Shabbat. A line of wagons and people on foot heads toward one small town. A tailor, a water carrier, a young scholar who has walked for days. They are not going to market. They are going to spend Shabbat at the table of their rebbe: to hear him teach, to sing, to eat a crumb from his plate. On Saturday night they will go home and tell everyone. That is how a movement travels. Today's word.
screen: `WAGONS ON A MUDDY ROAD.` → `SHABBAT AT THE REBBE'S TABLE.` → `HOME TO TELL EVERYONE.`

segments.voice: After the Baal Shem Tov died, much of his circle came to gather around one of his students, Rabbi Dov Ber, known as the Maggid of Mezeritch. A maggid is a preacher. Where the Baal Shem Tov had traveled from village to village, the Maggid mostly stayed put, and students came to him. He taught them in depth, and then, in effect, he sent them out. Each carried the teaching to a different region, and each became a rebbe with his own followers. Rabbi Elimelech went to Lizhensk in Galicia. Rabbi Shneur Zalman taught in the lands of White Russia and wrote a careful book of Hasidic thought, the Tanya. Rabbi Levi Yitzchak of Berditchev is remembered in the tales for defending ordinary Jews before God and finding the good in them. The shape that spread with them was new. A rebbe's court, where followers came for Shabbat and holidays. The tish, the rebbe's table, where he taught over food. The niggun, a melody often sung without words, rising and falling until the room was one voice. Stories passed hand to hand. And joy at the center, not as decoration but as a way to serve God. The Psalms have a line that fits those crowded tables: "Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!" Books came too, but much of the spreading happened the way joy does: one person comes home lit up, and the next week a neighbor comes along.
screen: `THE MAGGID OF MEZERITCH.` · `STUDENTS SENT OUT TO EACH REGION.` · `THE COURT, THE TABLE, THE NIGGUN.` · `HOW GOOD AND HOW PLEASANT.` · then, large: `JOY SPREADS.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: share one joy. Sit, and breathe easily. Let one good thing from this week come to mind, even a small one: a meal, a phone call, a song, a moment of quiet. Stay with it until you can feel it again. Then think of one person you could tell, or bring along next time. Picture their face when you tell them. If you like, hum a few notes of something, with or without words, and let the joy move. If you pray, you can give thanks in your own words. The bell holds the time.
Hasidism spreads. The Maggid of Mezeritch teaches students who carry the movement region by region, with its courts, tables, melodies and joy. Today's word.
Your line: joy spreads. Today, tell one person about one good thing, or bring someone along to something you love. Day nine hundred sixty-five.

966.title: The Vilna Gaon
966.hook: a great scholar of Talmud who opposed the new Hasidic movement
966.howItsDone: The Vilna Gaon's notes are printed in the margins of standard editions of the Talmud and other texts, and Lithuanian-style yeshivas still regard him as a model of devoted study.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hasidism spreads, from the Maggid's students to the rebbes' tables. Your line was joy spreads. Who did you tell about one good thing? Today the week ends with the man who stood against that movement. Day nine hundred sixty-six.

In Vilna, behind closed shutters, a lamp burns in the daytime. Inside, a man sits with a page of Talmud, and the stories say he kept the shutters shut so the street would not pull at his attention. He held no grand office. Yet letters came to him from far away, questions from rabbis who wanted his judgment, and people in the city spoke his name with a kind of awe. They gave him a title that means genius. Today, his name.
screen: `SHUTTERS CLOSED IN DAYLIGHT.` → `NO GRAND OFFICE.` → `A TITLE THAT MEANS GENIUS.`

segments.voice: Rabbi Elijah son of Solomon Zalman is remembered as the Vilna Gaon. Gaon was once the title of the heads of the great academies in Babylonia; in his day it became a word of honor for an extraordinary mind. Tradition says he held no official post as a rabbi in Vilna. He studied, mostly alone, and wrote notes and commentaries across the Bible, the Mishnah, the Talmud, Jewish law and the Kabbalah. He also studied grammar, mathematics and astronomy, because, he taught, they help a person understand the Torah. He lived the verse from Joshua: "thou shalt meditate therein day and night." Then the Hasidic movement reached Lithuania. The Gaon saw danger in it: rebbes whom followers seemed to treat as more than human, prayers said at changed times and in new ways, joy and ecstasy he feared would push aside careful study. He backed bans against the Hasidim. Hasidic tradition tells that Rabbi Shneur Zalman came to Vilna hoping to speak with him, and that the Gaon would not receive him. His followers came to be called Mitnagdim, the opponents. Hasidim and Mitnagdim argued for years, sometimes bitterly. Each side, in its own way, was guarding something it loved: for one, above all the joy of serving God; for the other, above all the discipline of learning. Hasidim studied too, and Mitnagdim prayed with feeling. Look back over this week: 1648 and the deep mire. A false messiah. A slow dawn after the fall. A council at the fair. A healer in the forests. Joy spreading. And now the genius of Vilna, with his shutters closed.
